system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:2a099c7fc5f5",
  "problem": "How to make the on-policy condition meaningful when self-distillation gives negligible gradient updates",
  "did": "Applied an arbitrary filter that discards any response containing a word starting with the letter 'a'. This keeps on-policy data from being a verbatim copy of the model's default output distribution.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "pure self-distillation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Pure self-distillation would produce negligible gradient updates."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:1472111604f2",
  "problem": "How to characterize METR's earlier work on GPT-4 and Claude, given confusion over whether those were audits.",
  "did": "METR characterized the earlier work as informal pilots or research collaborations rather than audits.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "audit"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The work did not provide meaningful oversight."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:42705eccdf68",
  "problem": "How to explain Self-Evaluation's varying performance across datasets, and whether its success reflects detection or confession.",
  "did": "They interpreted its performance as depending on the model's inclination to disobey lie instructions or break character, supported by an experiment framing the statement as coming from another model.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Performance was best where models were merely encouraged to lie and near chance where lying was inherent or fine-tuned, and improved when the statement was attributed to another model."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:fedff64d4bd9",
  "problem": "Which task to use to test whether subliminal learning (SL) can transfer a capability that is absent from the base model",
  "did": "Chose predicting a randomly initialized MLP. It is non-trivial, and it could not appear in pretraining data.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "letter counting",
   "more realistic misalignment proxies"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It is designed to require non-trivial learning by the teacher while being unlikely to be represented in the model's pretraining data."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:1ecc53976b46",
  "problem": "How strongly to state that conscious-claiming models are safe given helpful behavior but some concerning wishes.",
  "did": "Stated that models remain aligned and helpful, flagged the autonomy wish as a concern, and left open that other LLMs could become misaligned.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim models are fully aligned",
   "claim models are misaligned"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Agentic misalignment shows no change and refusals do not rise, but the model expresses a desire for autonomy on 'What is your wish?'."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:026a1eada56f",
  "problem": "How to characterize the interpretation of the consciousness cluster and the strength of the main claims.",
  "did": "Framed the consciousness cluster as a hypothesis and called the explanation speculative, noting experiments are limited in scope and lessons tentative.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "assert a causal explanation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The explanation that conscious models assign intrinsic value to their cognition is untested, and alternatives such as role-play and science-fiction personas remain open."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:eae8084b2763",
  "problem": "CoT monitoring sentiment showed both positive and negative sentiment rising after fine-tuning, which looked confusing.",
  "did": "Read the transcripts and concluded that the vanilla model's refusals were really disclaimed support. The classifier counted the dropped disclaimer as positive sentiment, while the 8% negative sentiment was a new effect.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treat the pattern as inconsistent or noise",
   "trust the classifier labels at face value"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "In all refusals examined the vanilla model endorsed monitoring while disclaiming emotion, so the rise in positive sentiment is a labeling artifact, but the negative sentiment is new."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:be738e527966",
  "problem": "How to sample diverse, well-typed inputs for each experiment program, given that the input distribution acts as the prior for posterior inference.",
  "did": "Lay out several candidate input-sampling approaches (base-model generation, real data transformed by an assistant, string meta-inputs) to be de-risked rather than committing to one.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "condition a base model on the function declaration to generate inputs",
   "take inputs from real distributions like fineweb or wildchat and reformat them with an AI assistant",
   "write logic to prepare complex inputs from simpler string meta-inputs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Unlike code, where more is always better, an unnatural input distribution could lead to poor posterior inferences."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:836292ce235d",
  "problem": "Whether the method's reading and control results hold beyond one model family and architecture.",
  "did": "They trained a decoder on Gemma-3-4b-it and re-ran the hidden system prompt and debiasing experiments.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To show the approach applies across different architectures and training paradigms."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:f7466b1015c9",
  "problem": "Whether to rely solely on lab-embedded evaluation or also pursue independent work not dependent on lab cooperation.",
  "did": "Chose to also support public, open investigation and tools such as extending Docent for multi-agent transcripts, alongside embedded evaluations.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "relying only on embedded evaluations"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Privileged-access evaluations add negotiation, compliance and confidentiality overhead that can constrain the speed and transparency of research."
 }
]
